items.title: RT by @Maks_NAFO_FELLA: The #Iranwar is already creating strategic opportunities for Russia. And Washington needs to understand what that means! The war has disrupted energy markets, driven up fuel prices and increased the value of alternative energy supplies. Now, Trump is temporarily easing sanctions on Russian diesel to deal with the fallout. Putin doesn't need to win every battle to benefit from this situation. When global energy markets are under pressure, Russia gains leverage! But here's the bigger issue: a stronger Russia benefits Iran! Moscow and Tehran are strategic partners. Their cooperation includes defence, security, energy and efforts to reduce dependence on Western financial systems. A Russia with greater economic flexibility and more room to manoeuvre is a more valuable partner for Tehran! It can deepen cooperation, help both countries navigate sanctions and complicate Western efforts to isolate Iran! This doesn't mean Russia will automatically rescue Iran. It means that strengthening Moscow can make the strategic challenge posed by Tehran harder to manage. And then there's Ukraine. If Ukraine is defeated or forced into submission, Russia gains far more than territory. Europe faces a much more dangerous security environment, NATO must prepare for greater risks, and Washington loses a key part of the security order that has served American interests for decades! A weaker Europe means a weaker Western alliance. And that is hardly in America's interest! Trump and his administration need to look at the bigger picture! You cannot view the Iran war, Russia's war against Ukraine and European security as separate problems! Short-term relief at the fuel pump may be politically attractive. But if the price is a stronger Russia, a more strategically supported Iran and a weaker Western alliance, is it really a good deal? Sometimes, the immediate solution creates the next strategic problem.

items.title: Ukraine's 7th Corps announces that it has shifted responsibility from the Pokrovsk area to Huliaipole area. The change happened in August.
items.summary:
Ukraine's 7th Corps announces that it has shifted responsibility from the Pokrovsk area to Huliaipole area. The change happened in August.
7th Corps of AAF (@7corpsDSHV)
The 7th Corps of the Ukrainian Air Assault Forces has taken over the Huliaipole direction as its area of responsibility.
This is one of the most critical sectors of the entire front. Here is why.
1. The road to Zaporizhzhia.
Huliaipole is less than 100 km from Zaporizhzhia, a city of strategic importance for the whole of southern Ukraine. The russian army sees Huliaipole as a staging ground for further offensive operations toward Zaporizhzhia. If the enemy gains a foothold here, it gains a springboard to push deeper into the region.
2. A hub for massing forces.
Urban environment allows the enemy to concentrate personnel and equipment, set up command posts, deploy artillery positions and establish launch sites for drone operators, all under cover of existing infrastructure. A town in enemy hands is a base from which offensive operations are prepared and sustained.
3. Logistical Node.
The Huliaipole–Polohy highway is one of the aggressors' key logistical artery in this sector. Ukrainian forces, 7th Corps' 237th drone batallion in particular, have already struck enemy equipment on it, including BM-21 Grad launchers. Whoever controls the roads controls the tempo of the fighting. Every disrupted convoy means fewer troops and less ammunition on the broader frontline.
4. A pressure point on the whole southern flank.
A breakthrough here would threaten neighbouring sectors, stretch Ukrainian defence and force the redeployment of reserves. Holding this line means protecting the entire depth of the defence behind it.
What the Corps brings:
The Corps comes with combat experience from the hardest sectors of the front and a "tech airborne" approach: drones, artillery, reconnaissance and assault units working as one system. Our task is to stabilise the line, wear down the enemy's offensive potential, cut his logistics and deny him the ability to use Huliaipole as a launchpad.
The map shows the disposition around Huliaipole and the key routes.

items.summaryUk:
Ukraine's 7th Corps announces that it has shifted responsibility from the Pokrovsk area to Huliaipole area. The change happened in August.
7th Corps of AAF (@7corpsDSHV)
The 7th Corps of the Ukrainian Air Assault Forces has taken over the Huliaipole direction as its area of responsibility.
This is one of the most critical sectors of the entire front. Here is why.
1. The road to Zaporizhzhia.
Huliaipole is less than 100 km from Zaporizhzhia, a city of strategic importance for the whole of southern Ukraine. The russian army sees Huliaipole as a staging ground for further offensive operations toward Zaporizhzhia. If the enemy gains a foothold here, it gains a springboard to push deeper into the region.
2. A hub for massing forces.
Urban environment allows the enemy to concentrate personnel and equipment, set up command posts, deploy artillery positions and establish launch sites for drone operators, all under cover of existing infrastructure. A town in enemy hands is a base from which offensive operations are prepared and sustained.
3. Logistical Node.
The Huliaipole–Polohy highway is one of the aggressors' key logistical artery in this sector. Ukrainian forces, 7th Corps' 237th drone batallion in particular, have already struck enemy equipment on it, including BM-21 Grad launchers. Whoever controls the roads controls the tempo of the fighting. Every disrupted convoy means fewer troops and less ammunition on the broader frontline.
4. A pressure point on the whole southern flank.
A breakthrough here would threaten neighbouring sectors, stretch Ukrainian defence and force the redeployment of reserves. Holding this line means protecting the entire depth of the defence behind it.
What the Corps brings:
The Corps comes with combat experience from the hardest sectors of the front and a "tech airborne" approach: drones, artillery, reconnaissance and assault units working as one system. Our task is to stabilise the line, wear down the enemy's offensive potential, cut his logistics and deny him the ability to use Huliaipole as a launchpad.
The map shows the disposition around Huliaipole and the key routes.

items.title: South Korea withdrawing the ambassador from Ukraine is one of the most bizarre moves I have seen in some time. Seoul even says that it received a letter from the Ukrainian foreign ministry which included an apology, but apparently it wasn’t enough. Ukraine is literally fighting South Korea’s primary enemy and the government in Seoul has nothing better to do than to yearn for an „extraordinary“ apology. Something very fishy is going on here and it has nothing to do with the North Korean soldier which Ukraine captured. The fact that it has been recently revealed that South Korean oil deliveries ended up in Russia is only one explanation. But I’m gonna be honest, not even that explains sufficiently the extreme lengths they are going.

items.title: RT by @DefMon3: "The first word brigade and corps commanders use to describe the first few months of Drapatyi's tenure is 'freedom'. Unlike his predecessor, who would tell some brigade commanders how and where to fight – even specifying the coordinates where a position should be set up – Drapatyi has chosen a different approach. He has opted to decentralize command, moving away from the 'micromanagement' that has already become widely known to the public... Ukrainska Pravda sources say the move away from hands-on management of brigades and corps has brought another change: Drapatyi no longer spends several hours every day hearing reports from all commanders, as Syrskyi did. 'Syrskyi would hear reports from everyone every day and could give specific instructions on how to respond to developments, including where troops should advance… Drapatyi doesn't do that; that's the job of the troop grouping commanders. Drapatyi focuses on strategic and systemic issues. And when commanders do speak to the commander-in-chief, he isn't interested in a standard report on 'what happened', but in statistics, analysing problems and finding solutions – in other words, what conditions need to be created for a particular commander to accomplish their mission. And that's the right approach,' a senior military officer told Ukrainska Pravda." https://www.pravda.com.ua/eng/news/2026/10/05/8056518/
